Ct. 2333 • 518 U.S. 651 • 1996 U.S. LEXIS 4264 Case holding summaries: • holding that the added restrictions on second habeas petitions are "well within the compass of this evolutionary process" and do not amount to a suspension of the writ • provision barring a writ of certiorari for review of grant or denial of certain habeas petitions did not unconstitutionally infringe on Supreme Court's constitutional authority because nothing in AEDPA impaired the Court's original jurisdiction to issue a writ of habeas corpus • discussing the “screening function” that courts must perform under the AEDPA • noting that repeals by implication are not favored • "[A]uthority to grant habeas relief to state prisoners is limited by § 2254, which specifies the conditions under which such relief may be granted to `a person in custody pursuant to the judgment of a State court.'" (citation omitted) • “[W]e assume, for purposes of decision here, that the Suspension Clause . . . refers to the writ as it exists today, rather than as it existed in 1789.” • AEDPA's restrictions on successive petitions "do not amount to a `suspension' of the writ" • noting that the writ originally only extended to prisoners in federal custody who were not “detained in prison by virtue of the judgment of a court” (citation and internal quotation marks omitted) • “The class of judicial actions reviewable by the writ [as known to the Framers] was more restricted as well.” • discussing history of the writ • implied repeals of habeas jurisdiction are disfavored • noting that AEDPA’s restric- tions on second or successive petitions "are well within the compass" of the evolution of the abuse of the writ doctrine • "The new restrictions on successive petitions constitute a modified res judicata rule, a restraint on what is called in habeas corpus practice 'abuse of the writ.' " • expressly leaving open the question whether and to what extent the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA) applies to original petitions • “[A]uthority to grant habeas relief to state prisoners is limited by § 2254, which specifies the conditions under which such relief may be granted to ‘a person in custody pursuant to the judgment of a State court.’” • AEDPA's restrictions on "second or successive" petitions constitute "a restraint on what is called in habeas corpus practice 'abuse of the writ'" • declining to find jurisdictional repeal by implication • AEDPA restrictions on second habeas petitions are within compass of evolving abuse-of-the-writ principles and do not amount to unconstitutional suspension of writ • the added restrictions which AEDPA places on second and successive petitions fall well within Congress' authority • AEDPA’s restrictions on successive petitions “do not amount to a ‘suspension’ of the writ” • declining to find jurisdictional repeal by implication • acknowledging that AEDPA “work[ed] substantial changes” to the ability of a federal tribunal to entertain a habeas petition • “[J]udgments about the proper scope
